body:
What happens if you do

```
$ env | grep ssh
```

Do you see something like this?

```
SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/tmp/ssh-Sj7JaoojWnEb/agent.3807
```

Do you see your keys if you do `ssh-add -l`?

I wonder If I'm using an outdated way of getting the agent [see blog post](http://blog.ralch.com/tutorial/golang-ssh-connection/)

```
$ env | grep -i ssh
SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/private/tmp/com.apple.launchd.3wxD7DaKDY/Listeners
```

```
$ ssh-add -l
The agent has no identities.
```

Oooohhh... Time to read that blog entry!

```
$ eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
Agent pid 54543
```

```
$ ssh-add -l
2048 SHA256:foo/BAR2342343fasdf ~/.ssh/id_rsa (RSA)
```

Hey, this time something's there. Maybe it'll work?

```
$ rclone-v1.35-158-g4652db3β-osx-amd64/rclone lsd seit:
          -1 2014-02-24 16:57:13        -1 .cache
          -1 2014-05-20 20:41:00        -1 my_project
          -1 2017-03-06 14:28:57        -1 .ssh
          -1 2014-05-20 20:42:36        -1 my_project.git
```
Success!

It seems like `ssh-agent` is an extra step which users will have to (know to) run. I don't know if `rclone` has any control over this, but would it be possible for it to launch `ssh-agent` if it isn't already running?

Thanks for working that out.  There must be a special macOS way of doing this...

A bit of searching [brings up this thread](https://github.com/lionheart/openradar-mirror/issues/15361) which has several work-arounds in it, probably the best is described [in this blog post](http://joshbuchea.com/revert-ssh-agent-behavior-pre-macos-sierra/)

Hi,

I, too, report this problematic issue with v 1.36

I've configured a SFTP remote to my remote Mac mini, specifying (passwordless) SSH.

I'm trying to connect to my remote Mac mini (macOS Sierra 10.12.1) from my laptop (macOS Sierra 10.12.3).

It fails with this message:

howardm$ rclone lsd Macmini:
2017/03/19 20:50:59 Failed to create file system for "Macmini:": couldn't connect ssh: ssh: handshake failed: ssh: unable to authenticate, attempted methods [none publickey], no supported methods remain

I can, obviously, connect to it otherwise via SSH in the usual way.

(It does work when I configure it with the `password` option)

I'm afraid I cannot understand the "workaround" described above.

Howard

@howardm there's definitely a bit of an issue with the workflow difference between doing `ssh` with keys and doing `ssh-agent`. I have found that the steps which work for me for scripting `rclone` from Matlab are as follows:

```
# It's important that you use `eval()`. Silly, I know, but that's the way ssh-agent works.
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

# Point toward your private ssh key. Mine was in ~/.ssh/id_rsa
ssh-add -K ~/.ssh/id_rsa 
.
.
.
# stuff here, like `rclone lsd Macmini:`
.
.
.

# Again, important to use `eval()`
eval "$(ssh-agent -k)"
```

Hmm. I'm very much a newbie at this, and still don't understand the process.

When I generated my private/public key combination, I didn't specify a passphrase (as best I remember). I certainly don't have to enter a passphrase for all the other `rsyncs` I use my pair for.

Thus, I don't understand the need for a ssh-agent here. Or, is this process needed here for rClone for some reason ?

___

As in: 

![01](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/6101226/24179956/dda40fbe-0e77-11e7-8060-053fa5f34763.png)

[From: https://help.github.com/articles/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent/]

Also, if I add it to ssh-agent (as described in the `Tip` in the screenshot above), is that a one-time thing/requirement only ?

Cheers,

Howard

> Thus, I don't understand the need for a ssh-agent here. Or, is this process needed here for rClone for some reason ?

`rclone` uses it, but I have limited experience with ssh so will defer to @ncw for explanations.

> Also, if I add it to ssh-agent (as described in the Tip in the screenshot above), is that a one-time thing/requirement only ?

You'll have to run the code I pasted every time you open a new terminal. It can get annoying because if you close the terminal without killing ssh-agent, it will continue to run in the background and it will never end. I solve that problem by periodically using `killall ssh-agent`.
Would it be helpful if rclone could use a key file directly without using ssh-agent?

I meant as a config option you would give a path to a key file, and rclone would load that instead of using the ssh-agent.  rclone could even copy the key file into the config file.

> How do tools like ssh, git, and rsync work? Do they load ssh-agent themselves, and make a best guess as to where the SSH keys are?

They would expect an ssh-agent to be running

> I meant as a config option you would give a path to a key file, and rclone would load that instead of using the ssh-agent. rclone could even copy the key file into the config file.

That would definitely work. Copying the key into the config file would be a cool, because then when I'm deploying my uploader tool I could copy only the conf file, instead of both it and the ssh key.

> They would expect an ssh-agent to be running

Gotcha. So I did a simple test to try to better understand how this works. When I `kill-all ssh-agent` and run `ssh foo.bar`, it loads ssh-agent. And when I open up another terminal, it uses the same ssh-agent. `git` does the same. So could `rclone` also launch `ssh-agent` and get keys in the same manner?

> So could rclone also launch ssh-agent and get keys in the same manner?

Oooh, interesting: http://rabexc.org/posts/pitfalls-of-ssh-agents. **Too many keys, github, and friends**.

So it looks like the most robust approach might be to have `rclone` load a new ssh-agent, add the key (perhaps saved in the config), and then kill it on exit.

FYI

I've used this method successfully:

1. ssh-add -K path/to/my_key  [needed once only]

2. Use this bash script for my scheduled backups

___
![pic](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/6101226/24276365/feed4b2e-0ffb-11e7-9722-dad344b6c290.jpg)
___

So the agent is killed after the sync or copy has finished.

Howard

@kubark42 
> So I did a simple test to try to better understand how this works. When I kill-all ssh-agent and run ssh foo.bar, it loads ssh-agent. And when I open up another terminal, it uses the same ssh-agent. git does the same. So could rclone also launch ssh-agent and get keys in the same manner?

I wonder where that behaviour of launching ssh-agent comes from because it certainly isn't standard ssh behaviour on linux.  I launch my ssh-agent once and I have to type in a very long password - it would be might annoying to have to do that on every rclone invocation!

I think this must be something to do with apple's integration of ssh keys into the secure keychain - that is what the `ssh-add -K` does in @howardm 's writeup above.  So I guess ssh-agent is just started as a shim for the secure keychain.  This must be OS X specific behaviour...

My theory is that this is done by the standard library.  When I cross compile rclone (which I do for the releases) it doesn't use the stdlib so you don't get this behaviour.  However if you compile rclone from source directly on OS X you will get this behaviour.

Can anyone confirm that?  If you need help compiling rclone from source there are some [brief instructions in the docs](http://rclone.org/install/#install-from-source).

If that is the case then I can look at getting the travis build to build the OSX binary...

> Can anyone confirm that? If you need help compiling rclone from source there are some brief instructions in the docs.

I just now built it from source and while it did launch `ssh-agent`, it was not able to connect. Adding the keys as per the above discussion, however, did allow the built-from-source binary to connect.

It seems like SSH key handling is annoyingly OS specific.

I don't know if this will provide some helpful diagnostic information:

I followed the [instructions in this post](http://joshbuchea.com/revert-ssh-agent-behavior-pre-macos-sierra/) about the ssh config file.

I thought I would then *not* have to use `ssh-add -A` in my script, as I mention above.

But my script doesn't work if it's not there.

Howard
